newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts moves to eliminate county governments.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts moves to eliminate county governments.

text.p: Massachusetts Gov. William Weld proposed a bill Tuesday to eliminate the more than 350-year-old system of county governments, transferring their essential functions to the state as of July 1, 1998.

Weld's decision to call for elimination of county governments follows a default late last year by Middlesex County on about $4.7 million of short-term debt. Since 1991, more than half the state's 14 counties have received some form of a state bail-out, totaling more than $25 million.

"Over the last 350 years, county government in this state has evolved into kind of a motley mess of departments and divisions without a coherent reason for being," Weld told reporters at the Mass. State House.
The bill calls for the state to assume all assets and liabilities of the counties, including county jails, houses of correction and courts.
A state commission will be created to make recommendations to the governor and the state Legislature on the future use of county hospitals, golf courses, parks, open space and airports.
Existing county assessments on cities and towns would be ended unless they were needed to pay off outstanding county debt.

"State taxpayers have footed the bill 22 times over the last six years to a tune of over $25 million," Weld said. "And even with that help, counties are precariously carrying over $45 million in debt and $125 million in unfunded pension liability."
Cities, towns and villages would be free to form "regional compacts" to better provide a limited number of services, he said.
The legislation would give the governor greater powers to deal with what he called recent fiscal crises in Middlesex and Worcester Counties.

The Mass. Secretary of Administration and Finance would be given the power to declare a county fiscal emergency and audit county finances, fix spending limits and put in place other financial controls. Counties also could be put in receivership.
